purpose: How each kind of sprinkler spreads its water with distance from the head (radial application profile), how that changes with pressure, what uniformity (DUlq) to expect, the makers' spacing rules and adjustment limits, and a wind rule of thumb - for rendering precipitation rate (in/h) on the lawn cell by cell.
howToUse: For a head with flow Q (gpm, as discharged at its arc setting), arc A (deg) and radius R (ft): mean rate over its wetted sector PRmean = 96.25 * Q * (360/A) / (pi * R^2) in/h, and the rate at distance r is PRmean * rel(r/R). rel is tabulated at rho = r/R = 0, 0.05, ..., rhoMax (1.0 unless stated); interpolate linearly; rel = 0 beyond rhoMax. With this normalization the water summed over the sector equals Q exactly, whatever the shape.

Pick typical[kind].rel for a head type, or a measured record (measured[]) when the user's head matches one. For a conventional fixed spray use sprayTraditionalAssumed (assumed), or typical['spray-high-efficiency'] for Toro Precision / Rain Bird HE-VAN / similar.

Radius: the catalog radius at the head's pressure (heads/*.json rows). The CIT radius is the ASAE S398.1 'distance of throw' (furthest catch of at least 0.01 in/h), which matches the catalog to within a foot or two for rotors.

A head whose radius is turned down with its screw or ring keeps roughly its flow and puts it on a smaller circle. No profile of a reduced-radius head was found. Assume the same shape scaled to the new R (assumed), and expect more water near the head (the diffuser breaks the stream up).
Partial arcs: use the same radial profile across the sector. Measured grids show the straight edges of a part-circle pattern are lighter and ragged, which this ignores.

conventions.rho: r / R, where R is the radius stated in the record (CIT tested radius for radial tests; catalog radius for the spray grids; end of the plotted curve for the Hunter MP plots).
conventions.rel: local application rate divided by the area-weighted mean rate over the wetted area: integral from 0 to rhoMax of rel(rho)*2*rho d rho = 1 (checked to 1.00 for every array). rel = 1 everywhere would be a perfectly flat (uniform) disc.
conventions.innerHalfShare: fraction of the head's water landing inside r < R/2 (flat disc 0.25, triangular 0.50). Our single-number index of centre weighting; it rises with pressure (water falls closer in) and falls at low pressure (doughnut).
conventions.catchToFlowRatio: water caught (integrated over the arc tested) divided by the tested flow. It is near 1 for many CIT tests, and near 2 for some 360-degree rotor tests (probably run part-circle, or stored on another scale). This is why every profile was renormalized and only its SHAPE is used. A record with a ratio far from 1 has a doubtful absolute scale, but its shape is still sound.
conventions.status tags: measured = catch-can numbers from a lab (CIT) or a maker; derived = our arithmetic on measured numbers (normalization, ring-averaging, digitizing, averaging, overlap simulation); assumed = a shape we chose to match a published description, with no measured numbers behind it.

cit-radial.what: Sprinkler profile files (SPACE .PRF format) published free by the Center for Irrigation Technology (CIT), California State University Fresno: single-leg radial catch-can tests in CIT's zero-wind indoor lab. Fixed 500-byte records with these fields: lab, date, time, maker, model, nozzle, psi, -, gpm, catch spacing (ft), radius (ft), arc (deg), rotation time (min), -, test no., duration (min), provider, -, number of catches, then the catch values. The first value repeats the first catch (a stand-in for r = 0); value i is at r = i x spacing. Values are in/h x 1000 (the last wet catch is 0.010 in/h at the stated radius, the ASAE S398.1 throw definition, and the radial volume of three of the four Hunter G90 golf records and all 24 Hunter PGJ records comes within 7% of the tested flow).
cit-radial.index: https://jcast.fresnostate.edu/cit/goods/profiles.html ('The Center for Irrigation Technology now offers all of its sprinkler profiles free of charge'; index of makers at https://jcast.fresnostate.edu/cit/goods/citprofiles.html)
files: https://jcast.fresnostate.edu/cit/documents/software/cit.zip (HUNTER.PRF: I-20 2001-2004; RAINBIRD.PRF: 5000 RC 2004 and ag impacts 2005)
cit-radial.format: Undocumented on the page; we inferred it from the files, and the flow cross-check supports the inference. Positions could be offset by half a catch spacing (1-2 ft) if CIT stores catch centres differently. That does not change the shapes materially.
cit-radial.accessNote: jcast.fresnostate.edu serves a chain ending at emSign Root CA - G1. Fetch with a CA bundle that includes it (Mozilla's/certifi does).

cit-grid.what: CIT full-grid catch tests of ONE half-circle spray nozzle (files .dta / .dtm): header (columns, rows, ...), date, provider, product, psi, gpm, duration (min), nozzle; then columns x rows catch values with 9999 at the head (head at the middle of the straight edge). Values = catch depth x 1000 over the test duration (in/h x 1000 for the 60-minute tests). Cell size 1 ft (2 ft for the 15H file) - inferred, and the volume check gives 0.77-1.13 of the tested flow.
cit-grid.derivation: We averaged the cells into 1-ft rings (2 ft for 15H) about the head, using only cells 20-160 deg from the straight edge. Then we normalized on the catalog radius out to rho = 1.3.

hunter-mp-design-guide.what: Hunter MP Rotator Design Guide, 'Uniformity Samples': precipitation rate (in/h) vs distance (ft) for MP1000-90, MP2000-90 and MP3000-90 at 180 deg and 40 psi, 'from tests performed indoors in controlled conditions'. It also has CU and DU vs square spacing for each.
hunter-mp-design-guide.derivation: The plots are vector graphics. We converted the page to SVG (pdftocairo), took the filled profile paths, calibrated against the axis tick marks (4.806 pt per ft) and sampled at rho steps of 0.05. Our overlap simulation of the digitized MP2000 profile gives DUlq 0.92/0.87/0.83/0.81 at 16/18/20/22 ft square spacing; Hunter's plot shows 0.88/0.86/0.77/0.75. For MP1000 we get 0.93/0.89/0.92/0.80 at 10/12/14/16 ft (Hunter 0.85/0.82/0.83/0.73); for MP3000 0.86/0.81/0.81 at 27/29/31 ft (Hunter 0.84/0.79/0.81). The same trend, about 3-8 points higher, which validates the digitizing.

rotor.status: derived: arithmetic mean of the family means below (each family mean is the mean of its normalized measured profiles), renormalized to mean 1

simulatedOverlap.status: derived: our overlap simulation, square layout of full-circle heads at spacing S (R = the profile's radius), zero wind, every head identical, 24x24 sample grid per cell; an upper bound for the field, not a prediction

rotor.shape: Gear-driven rotors with standard (about 25 deg) nozzles at the maker's recommended or nearest tested pressure. Shape: a spike within about 0.1 R of the head (the first catch can, 1-2 ft out; it carries little volume because the area there is small), then a broad, nearly flat shoulder (rel 1.0-1.5) to about 0.8 R, often a small second hump at 0.8-0.9 R (strongest for Rain Bird 5000 RC and Toro T5), then a steep fall to zero at R. Between 'flat' and 'triangular': the inner half of the radius gets 0.28-0.38 of the water by family (flat 0.25, triangular 0.50). No PGP (original) or Rain Bird 3500/32SA test was available; the I-20 shares its nozzle set with the PGP Ultra (see heads/hunter-rotors.json).

rotor-low-angle.status: derived: arithmetic mean of the family means below (each family mean is the mean of its normalized measured profiles), renormalized to mean 1

simulatedOverlap.status: derived: our overlap simulation, square layout of full-circle heads at spacing S (R = the profile's radius), zero wind, every head identical, 24x24 sample grid per cell; an upper bound for the field, not a prediction

rotor-low-angle.shape: Toro T5 low-angle (10 deg) nozzles: a bigger spike at the head and a flatter, slightly outward-weighted body than the standard nozzles.

rotary-nozzle.status: derived: arithmetic mean of the family means below (each family mean is the mean of its normalized measured profiles), renormalized to mean 1

simulatedOverlap.status: derived: our overlap simulation, square layout of full-circle heads at spacing S (R = the profile's radius), zero wind, every head identical, 24x24 sample grid per cell; an upper bound for the field, not a prediction

rotary-nozzle.shape: Multi-stream multi-trajectory (MSMT) rotary nozzles. Hunter's published MP profiles are close to a wedge (MP1000, MP2000: rel falls almost linearly from the head to R) and the MP3000 adds a near-head peak and a long flat tail; Toro PRN is lumpier (individual streams show as bumps at 0.2-0.6 R). Inner half share 0.42-0.57 (MP) and 0.38-0.47 (PRN at 40 psi): the most centre-weighted of the types, closest to the textbook triangle. No Rain Bird R-VAN or K-Rain RN profile was found.

spray-high-efficiency.status: derived: arithmetic mean of the family means below (each family mean is the mean of its normalized measured profiles), renormalized to mean 1

simulatedOverlap.status: derived: our overlap simulation, square layout of full-circle heads at spacing S (R = the profile's radius), zero wind, every head identical, 24x24 sample grid per cell; an upper bound for the field, not a prediction

spray-high-efficiency.shape: ONLY newer high-efficiency spray nozzles were measured (Toro Precision Series, which is an oscillating-stream 'H2O chip' nozzle, and Rain Bird HE-VAN). They were normalized on the catalog radius. Toro Precision wets beyond it to about 1.1-1.2 R; HE-VAN stops at about 1.0 R (HE-VAN 12 at about 11 ft). Toro: lower at the head (rel about 1.0), peak at 0.3-0.4 R, then roughly linear to zero near 1.1 R. HE-VAN: a strong close-in peak within 0.15 R (Rain Bird markets HE-VAN for 'close-in' watering) and a shoulder (rel 1.6-1.8) to 0.5 R, falling to zero by about 1.0 R. NOT representative of conventional deflector sprays (Rain Bird MPR/U-series, Hunter Pro, Toro 570 MPR+); for those see sprayTraditionalAssumed.

impact.shape: Rain Bird agricultural impact sprinklers 14VH, 20JH, 30FH and 30WH (CIT tests supplied by growers' groups) stand in for residential impact heads (Rain Bird 2045 Maxi-Paw, 25BPJ). No residential impact head profile was found. Shape: a strong near-head spike (the range tube and drive-arm spoon break part of the stream), a flat body (rel 0.9-1.1) to 0.85 R, a mild outer hump, then a fall to zero.

sprayTraditionalAssumed.status: ASSUMED. No measured radial profile of a conventional fixed-deflector spray nozzle (Rain Bird MPR or U-Series, Hunter Pro Fixed/Pro Adjustable, Toro 570 MPR+) was found.
sprayTraditionalAssumed.basis: Rain Bird patent US 7,234,651 B2 (Mousavi & Yarala, 'Close-in irrigation spray head', granted 2007-06-26), background, col. 1 lines 51-67: spray heads 'have typically produced distribution patterns which have a maximum fall-out commencing approximately two feet radially away from the spray head, and thereafter reducing to zero at the maximum distance of throw', with 'little or no appreciable water' within about two feet - an arcuate 'dead zone'; 'it is common practice in the industry to install the spray heads ... two feet closer together than would otherwise be necessary.' Mecham (2006) photographed off-the-shelf 10, 12 and 15 ft nozzles on wetted asphalt. 'A few of the nozzles had excellent coverage for the pattern intended, but most were not as good as would have been expected'. He found 'very little water falling' at the dry edges and near the corners, and suggested that nozzles 'do not throw the water as far as expected'.
sprayTraditionalAssumed.formula: g(rho) = 0.1 + 0.9*rho/rho0 for rho < rho0; g = (1 - rho)/(1 - rho0) for rho0 <= rho <= 1; rel = g normalized numerically (integral of rel*2*rho = 1). rho0 = 2 ft / R (the patent's two feet).
caveats: The patent is Rain Bird describing its competitors and its own older heads in order to sell a fix; it gives no numbers beyond 'about two feet'.
Measured newer sprays (Toro Precision, HE-VAN, typical['spray-high-efficiency']) do NOT have the dead zone. Toro Precision is lowest at the head but still about half its peak at 1 ft.

Mecham (2006) suspected the throw is often shorter than the catalog radius, while the CIT grids for Toro Precision wet 10-20% beyond it and HE-VAN about to it. Treat R itself as uncertain by about +/-15% for sprays.

analyticShapes.conventions: rel(rho), rho = r/R, normalized so that the integral of rel(rho)*2*rho d rho from 0 to 1 is 1 (area-weighted mean over the wetted circle = 1), as for the measured profiles.

triangular.status: textbook shape (Christiansen 1942 type B as reproduced in Pair et al. 1983; the '30 degree wedge' that Rain Bird's design manual and Rain Bird patent US 7,234,651 call ideal)
triangular.use: The idealized profile; head-to-head square spacing gives near-perfect overlap (our simulation: DUlq 0.95 at S = R, 0.85 at 1.2 R, 0.58 at 1.4 R). Real heads are flatter than this, so it overstates how forgiving head-to-head spacing is.

elliptical.status: textbook shape (Christiansen type C, 'elliptical'); Fedler & Borrelli (2001) describe gear-drive heads at recommended pressure as giving 'a nice elliptical distribution pattern'

peaked.status: assumed analytic stand-in for Christiansen type A (peak at the head, concave flanks) - the high-pressure / misting direction (water falls close in, throw shortens)

flat.status: textbook shape (Christiansen type F, rectangular); a lower bound on centre weighting

doughnut.status: assumed analytic stand-in for Christiansen type E ('doughnut'): the low-pressure shape, dry near the head, ring of heavy water at 0.5-0.8 R. Shape chosen by us to look like the textbook sketch; no measured residential doughnut was found

summary: MEASURED (CIT series, measured[] / table below): raising pressure moves water INWARD. For rotors and rotary nozzles, the share of water inside R/2 rises with pressure: Rain Bird 5000 2.5RC 0.26 / 0.31 / 0.32 at 30 / 40 / 50 psi; Toro T5 1.5 nozzle 0.24 -> 0.35 from 25 to 65 psi; Toro PRN-TA #3 0.35 -> 0.51 from 30 to 75 psi. Lowering pressure moves water OUTWARD. At the bottom of the range (25-30 psi) Rain Bird 5000 and Toro T5 standard nozzles grow an outer ring at 0.85-0.95 R with rel 1.6-2.3 (compared with 0.9-1.3 at recommended pressure) and a trough of 0.5-0.8 at 0.5-0.7 R: the start of the textbook doughnut. Hunter I-20 and PGJ shift the same way but less (inner-half share up 0.00-0.09 from 30 to 50 psi) and show no strong outer ring at 30 psi.

MEASURED: radius grows with pressure across the tested ranges (e.g. PRN-TA #3 14 -> 24 ft from 30 to 75 psi; T5 4.0 nozzle 36 -> 44 ft from 25 to 65 psi; 5000 2.5RC 36 -> 38 ft from 30 to 50 psi). The charts in heads/*.json give the maker's radius for each pressure. No measured case of throw SHORTENING at high pressure was found for these heads within their tested ranges.

TEXTBOOK (Christiansen 1942 profile family A-F, via Pair et al. 1983 'Sprinkler Irrigation' 5th ed., Fig. reproduced as Fig. 7 in Fedler & Borrelli 2001): A peaked at the head with concave flanks, B triangular, C elliptical, D flat-topped, E doughnut (low centre, ring at mid-radius), F rectangular. At spacing 50% of the wetted diameter, Christiansen's uniformity coefficient of 85 is achievable 'except when the distribution pattern is a donut shape'. 'A donut shape is an indication of the sprinkler head being operated at a pressure lower than recommended' (Fedler & Borrelli 2001, p. 27). For gear-drive heads: 'If the pressure is too low, the stream will not break apart to obtain adequate water distribution thus giving a donut-shaped distribution' (p. 15). High pressure makes a greater percentage of small droplets and more drift (p. 13).

FIELD (sprays): Mecham (2006), 86 catch-can tests of 12 and 15 ft spray nozzles: average DUlq 57.25% at 30 psi vs 55.6% at 45 psi, and flow 17.8% higher at 45 psi (some nozzles had pressure-compensating discs). A 12 ft fixed-arc zone measured DUlq 62% / 58% / 53% at 30 / 45 / 60 psi, with precipitation 1.70 / 1.91 / 2.17 in/h; 'At 60 psi, the misting of the nozzle was significant'. 15 ft nozzles were less affected by high pressure than 12 ft ones. Same nozzle at 30 and 45 psi photographed: 'higher pressure will affect it adversely, but ... that may not necessarily be the case'.

EXTENSION: Oklahoma State HLA-6617 (Moore & Moss 2019), already in PRACTICE.md: high pressure - 'the water leaves the nozzle as a fine mist instead of large droplets. Carried away by the wind, the fine mist evaporates' (a spray example at 30 psi 3.3 gpm vs 50 psi 4.8 gpm); low pressure - heads may not pop up, water 'will not reach adjacent heads', 'donut-shaped zones of brown grass around a sprinkler head'. EPA WaterSense spray-body background (2017): higher operating pressure causes 'excessive flow rates, misting, fogging, uneven coverage'.

NOT FOUND: any measured radial profile of a conventional spray nozzle above 30 psi, so the misting shift (water falling short, close in) cannot be quantified for sprays here. ASSUMED for the model: between the recommended pressure and +50% above it, blend the spray profile toward analyticShapes.peaked and shorten R. The size of that shortening is not sourced. Below the recommended pressure, blend toward analyticShapes.doughnut for rotors and impacts and shorten R per the heads/*.json chart.
pressure.modelSuggestion: derived from the CIT series: for rotors and rotary nozzles within their charted ranges, prefer the measured record at the nearest tested psi. Otherwise interpolate between two tested pressures of the same nozzle. Outside the tested range, do not extrapolate the shape, only flag it.

uniformity.definition: DUlq = mean of the lowest quarter of catch-can depths / mean of all (Merriam & Keller 1978, as quoted by Colasurdo et al. 2011).

ratingsIA.source: Mecham 2004 (quoting IA Turf & Landscape Irrigation BMPs Feb 2004 and IA auditor training manuals) [read]
ratingsIA.bmpMinimum: IA BMP (2004): fixed spray at least 0.55, rotors at least 0.70.
ratingsIA.auditorManual2010: IA Certified Landscape Irrigation Auditor manual (Sept 2010), sprays: 0.65-0.75 achievable, 0.55-0.65 target, 0.45-0.55 historical (quoted by Colasurdo et al. 2011) [read, 2nd-hand quote]

mecham2004.source: Mecham, B. (2004) 'Using Distribution Uniformity to Evaluate the Quality of a Sprinkler System', IA Technical Conference, Table 'Sprinkler System Performance' [read]

residential.note: printed in the fixed-spray column; the text does not say whether rotor zones are included

residential.where: Univ. of Florida case study (grid of hundreds of cans)

mecham2004.conclusion: 'the average DULQ is about 50% no matter what type of sprinkler head is being used'. Usually only the best one or two zones per yard were audited, so the true whole-system DU is lower. Pitts et al. (1996), California: residential average DU 49%, with more than 40% of systems below 40%.

baum2005.source: Baum, Dukes & Miller (2005) 'Analysis of residential irrigation distribution uniformity', J. Irrig. Drain. Eng. 131(4):336-341 [2nd: abstract via search summaries and Kumar et al. 2014; full text not reachable]
baum2005.values: Florida residences, full-coverage catch grids: mean DUlq 0.45; rotor zones 0.49 vs fixed-spray zones 0.41 (spray range 0.12-0.67). Controlled plots: rotors 0.55, sprays 0.49 (quarter-circle nozzles only). Fixed quarter-circle spray nozzles did better than adjustable ones. The authors say uniformity could be improved by avoiding low pressure and by proper spacing. The grid method gave lower DU than the Mobile Irrigation Lab 16-24-can method: 43.4% vs 55.1% on the same 19 homes (Mecham 2004 quoting Baum et al. 2003).

controlledTests.status: measured (designed test plots, mostly < 5 mph wind)
items: Mecham 2006 (Northern Colorado Water Conservancy District, asphalt pad, 86 tests, 12 and 15 ft spray nozzles, square / triangle / equilateral layouts): DUlq 0.29-0.78; best 0.76 (15 ft, square, 30 psi) and 0.78 (12 ft variable-arc, equilateral, 30 psi); average 0.5725 at 30 psi, 0.556 at 45 psi. Variable-arc nozzles gave the lowest values (0.29-0.43). [read]

Colasurdo, Kumar & Vis 2011 (Cal Poly Pomona; Toro Precision, Hunter Pro and Rain Bird MPR 12 and 15 ft; 9-nozzle square system; 30 psi; 222 tests): mean DUlq 0.61 (12 ft 0.62, 15 ft 0.60). The high-efficiency nozzle ('brand B') averaged 0.65, the others 0.55-0.64. Spacing +/-30% of head-to-head barely changed DU, except 15 ft at +30% (0.55). No nozzle had its best DU at the recommended spacing. [read; brands anonymized in the results]

Kumar, Green, Vis, Parkins & Perera 2014 (Cal Poly Pomona; three MSMT rotary nozzles at 40 psi; 9-nozzle square system on turf; 60 tests): DUlq 0.54 at maximum (head-to-head) spacing; 0.62 / 0.66 at 10% / 25% closer spacing with the radius unadjusted; 0.70 / 0.72 with the radius screw turned down to reach the next head. Low-half DU 0.71-0.82. Nozzles A/B/C at max spacing: 0.58/0.58/0.45. [read]

Hattendorf & Crookston 2011 (NCWCD, 30x15 ft indoor system): MP2000 at 40 psi DUlq 0.79-0.81; Toro Precision spray 15 ft at 32 psi 0.75-0.78; Toro PRN at 30 psi 0.49-0.50 with can tips at ground level vs 0.69-0.70 with can rims at ground level - the 20 deg stream hits the cans. [read]

makerClaims.status: manufacturer statements (indoor / zero wind, chosen spacing)
items: Rain Bird rotary nozzle reference sheet (rainbird.com/media/4124): R-VAN (8-24 ft) and R-Series 'DU(LQ) > 0.70'; 'The average DU(LQ) of the applicable products exceed 0.65'; meet ASABE/ICC 802-2014. [read]
Rain Bird HE-VAN product page: average DUlq 70%, scheduling coefficient <= 1.6 [2nd, search summary of https://www.rainbird.com/products/he-van-high-efficiency-variable-arc-nozzles]

Hunter MP Rotator Design Guide (2016, 2020): DU 0.85 -> 0.73 (MP1000, 10 -> 16 ft square), 0.88 -> 0.75 (MP2000, 16 -> 22 ft), 0.84 -> 0.79 (MP3000, 27 -> 31 ft), indoors (read off the vector plot). [read]

Toro Variable Radius Precision Series spray (EMEA catalogue p. 18, 2016): DU 0.54-0.58, CU 0.73-0.75, SC 1.2-1.4 at 2.0 bar for 2.4-4.6 m radii. [read, https://cdn.thetorocompany.com/api/assetstorage/623_37cb9b68-69d6-4392-adf1-abf925b5bb87]

uniformity.simulatedFromProfiles: derived: see typical[*].simulatedOverlap. With perfect heads in zero wind at head-to-head square spacing: rotors 0.73, rotary nozzles 0.90, high-efficiency sprays 0.88, impacts 0.69. Field audits are 0.40-0.58 for all types. The gap (wind, pressure, tilt, mismatched heads, spacing, blocked heads) is larger than the differences between types. That agrees with Mecham 2004: 'Type or brand of equipment has the least impact on performance quality compared to proper design ..., installation and maintenance.'

suggestedDefaults.status: derived/assumed - our pick from the field audits above, for flagging a lawn's expected evenness when the user has no audit
suggestedDefaults.why: The spray, rotor and impact values are the medians of the audit averages above (sprays 0.41-0.55, rotors 0.41-0.58). The rotary-nozzle value is assumed: Kissinger & Solomon 2005 (IA conference; quoted in Vis, Kumar & Mitra 2008) found an 18-point DU gain when sprays were swapped for rotary nozzles, and the MSMT plot tests at head-to-head spacing gave 0.54-0.81. No large field audit of rotary-nozzle zones was found.

spacing.headToHead: Rain Bird Landscape Irrigation Design Manual (2000) p. 41 [read]: 'Head-to-head, or 50% sprinkler spacing, is the most common spacing used in landscape irrigation. Where winds are a threat to good coverage, spacing as close as 40% may be required.' Rain Bird spray and rotary-nozzle charts compute precipitation for 'Square spacing based on 50% diameter of throw' and 'Triangular spacing based on 50% diameter of throw' [read]. Hunter: 'MP Rotators are recommended for use with head-to-head coverage in either square or triangular layouts' (MP Design Guide 2016 p. 3) [read].
spacing.maximum: Rain Bird LIDM p. 41 [read]: the first 60% of the radius is 'generally sufficiently irrigated', so the maximum recommended spacing is 60% of diameter (each head's 60%-of-radius line meets its neighbour's); the ideal distribution curve 'should ideally look like a 30 degree slope coming down from the sprinkler location - a wedge'. Our measured profiles are flatter than that wedge (rotor family means put 0.28-0.38 of their water inside R/2, a wedge 0.50); rotary nozzles (0.43-0.51) come closest to it.

byLayoutAndWind.squareDiagonal: In square spacing at 50%, the diagonal between opposite corner heads is over 70% of diameter - the usual weak spot at the centre of the square.

spacing.evidenceOnCloser: Kumar et al. 2014 (MSMT nozzles): spacing 10-25% closer than head-to-head raised DUlq from 0.54 to 0.62-0.72. Colasurdo et al. 2011 (sprays): +/-30% made little difference, except 15 ft at +30%. Rain Bird patent US 7,234,651: the industry spaces conventional sprays 'two feet closer together than would otherwise be necessary' to cover the near-head dead zone. [read]
spacing.outdoorAgricultural: For context: Fedler & Borrelli (2001) recommend 0.5 x wetted diameter on both axes for wastewater spray fields, and say a Christiansen CU of 85 is then achievable except with doughnut patterns [read]. USDA NRCS Code 442 allows 50-75% of the wetted diameter along laterals for agriculture [2nd].

adjustment.note: Limits as the makers print them. A reduced radius keeps most of the flow (the screw throttles and diffuses), so the precipitation rate rises roughly with (R_full/R_set)^2 if the flow is unchanged. Rain Bird and Hunter both note the chart flow is for the unreduced nozzle, and that the screw 'may be required' to reach catalog radius. The flow at a reduced radius is not charted, except for the Hunter MP800SR min-radius columns and the Toro PCD spray (heads/*.json).

wind.ruleOfThumb: Rain Bird LIDM pp. 42-43 [read]: square layouts 55% of diameter at 0-3 mph, 50% at 4-7, 45% at 8-12; triangles 60/55/50%; rectangles keep 60% along the wind and close across it to 50/45/40%. As close as 40% where winds threaten coverage (p. 41). Wind moves the weak spot of a square pattern off centre (p. 42).
wind.heightCorrection: Fedler & Borrelli (2001) p. 14 [read]: wind at sprinkler height (< 3.3 ft) is about 0.75 x the 11.5-13 ft weather-station value. Night-time wind is about 0.67 x the daily average (Jensen et al. 1990), so night watering sees about 0.5 x the reported average.
wind.testConditions: All profiles here are zero-wind (CIT indoor; Hunter indoor). The IA audit and SWAT spray-nozzle protocols run below 5 and 3 mph (SWAT Spray Head Nozzle protocol v3.2, 2015, s. 7.1; Mecham 2006) [read].
wind.nozzleChoice: Makers claim low trajectories and thick streams resist wind (Rain Bird R-VAN: 'Thick streams + Low Trajectory = Maximum Wind Resistance'; Hunter Pro Fixed: 'Large water droplets minimize misting'; Toro PRN: 'Maximum trajectory height of 20 deg to help fight wind') [read, maker claims]. Vis, Kumar & Mitra (2008, IA tech. conf.): about 75% of runoff from spray-nozzle plots was wind drift, and rotary nozzles reduced it [read, abstract].

testMethods: Single-leg radial test: cans at equal intervals along one or more radial legs from one head in zero wind; the profile ('distribution rate curve', DRC) is entered into CIT's SPACE program to simulate overlap ('densogram') and compute CU, DU and SC for any spacing (Rain Bird 'Putting Rain Bird Sprinkler Test Data To Work, Using The SPACE Program', 2003, https://www.rainbird.com/sites/default/files/2016-10/models/documentsagts_SPACE.pdf; Rain Bird LIDM p. 41) [read]. SPACE = Sprinkler Profile And Coverage Evaluation, developed at CIT in 1988.

Distance of throw: 'furthest point of water application at least equal to 0.01 in./h (0.3 mm/h) as per ASAE 398.1' (SWAT Spray Head Sprinkler Nozzles testing protocol v3.2, s. 4.5, https://www.irrigation.org/IA/FileUploads/SWAT/Spray-Head-Nozzles-Testing-Protocol-Version-3.2-4-28-2015.pdf) [read]. ASAE S398.1 and ISO 15886-3 themselves were not read (paywalled).

SWAT spray-nozzle protocol (2015): no radial profile. It tests each nozzle against claimed flow and throw, then 9-head square (4 Q, 4 H, 1 F) and 7-head circular arrangements, nozzles 4 in above the cans, wind < 3 mph, reporting DUlq and an operational efficiency [read].
ASABE/ICC 802-2014 (landscape sprinkler standard) is cited by Rain Bird for its DUlq claims (> 0.65); not read.

notes: HARD (measured): CIT radial profiles for Hunter I-20 (19 tests), Hunter PGJ (24), Rain Bird 5000 RC (12), Toro T5 standard (40) and low-angle (19), Toro PRN (20) and Rain Bird ag impacts (11); CIT full-grid tests for Toro Precision spray 5H-15H and Rain Bird HE-VAN 12/15 at 30 psi; Hunter's own MP1000/2000/3000 profiles at 40 psi. Everything else in typical, the simulations, the pressure summaries and suggestedDefaults is derived or assumed, as labelled.

NOT FOUND (asked for, searched): radial profiles for Rain Bird MPR / U-Series, Hunter Pro Fixed / Pro Adjustable, Toro 570 MPR+ (conventional sprays), Rain Bird R-VAN, Hunter PGP (original) / PGP Ultra (the I-20 shares its nozzles), residential impact heads, and any spray profile above 30 psi. CIT says older profile files that 'WERE listed here before' are available on request at cit.office@mail.fresnostate.edu - the most promising next step for MPR/U-series/R-VAN shapes. Hunter I-25 commercial rotor profiles are in hunteri25.zip and were not included. Keller & Bliesner's Sprinkle and Trickle Irrigation (1990) and Solomon's work were not reachable; their profile shapes are represented here via Christiansen/Pair as reproduced by Fedler & Borrelli.

DOUBT - normalization: CIT absolute catch values disagree with the tested flow by up to a factor of about 2 for some 360-degree rotor tests (catchToFlowRatio). Only shapes are used, so this does not affect rel. Hunter's plotted MP rates integrate to 53-72% of chart flow - shape only.

DOUBT - near-head values: rel at rho = 0 and 0.05 rests on one catch can 1-2 ft from the head and is often large (2-7). Over a 1 ft cell this matters; over the lawn it carries little volume. Clamp it when rendering, e.g. average rel over the first cell. The spray-grid head cell is unmeasured, so rho = 0 there copies the 1-ft ring.

DOUBT - lab vs field: every profile is zero-wind, new nozzle, vertical riser, regulated pressure. Field DUlq (0.40-0.58) is far below what these profiles simulate (0.69-0.90 at head-to-head). Use the audit-based defaults to set expectations, and the profiles to show WHERE dry and wet bands fall.

DOUBT - typical rotor average mixes four makers whose shapes differ (Rain Bird 5000 RC has the strongest outer hump; I-20 is the most centre-weighted). Use the family records when the user's rotor is known.
The core of this file (CIT data) is public test data from a university lab; Hunter and Rain Bird material is maker literature (claims), and is labelled so. No addresses or personal data.
